***

Former Liberal minister Philip Ruddock has been appointed by the Australian government to review whether current laws sufficiently protect the human right to religious freedom. The appointment, announced on Wednesday, aims to preempt a contentious debate over religious amendments in an upcoming same-sex marriage bill. However, Treasurer Scott Morrison emphasized that the review is not a replacement for those amendments, signaling ongoing divisions within the government.

Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull framed the review as a necessary step following Australia’s "yes" vote on marriage equality and the impending legislation. He stressed the importance of carefully examining religious freedom protections, noting that many proposed reforms extend beyond the scope of marriage and could have broader implications. Turnbull warned against hasty legislative changes, citing risks of unintended consequences.

The debate over timing has split senior conservatives, with figures like Peter Dutton and Mathias Cormann advocating for a separate religious freedom bill next year. In contrast, Morrison and Liberal Senator David Fawcett have pushed for simultaneous consideration alongside the marriage equality legislation. This divide highlights the government’s struggle to balance competing priorities.

Turnbull cautioned against adopting broad, bill-of-rights-style declarations, which he argued could create legal uncertainties. He described the review as a "timely expert stocktake" to guide any future legislative reforms, ensuring protections are carefully tailored. The government’s focus is on avoiding overreach while addressing concerns raised by religious groups.

Ruddock, who previously served as Australia’s special envoy for human rights, has been tasked with delivering his findings by 31 March. Turnbull praised his experience, suggesting his expertise will help navigate the complex intersection of religious freedom and marriage equality. The review’s outcome will shape the government’s next steps in this politically sensitive area.
